text: Welcome everyone. Today we are looking at common failure patterns in concurrent, stateful systems, and more importantly, how to reason about them like an engineer rather than just a coder. The big idea is that a design can look fine in a happy-path demo and still fail under pressure. Our job is to identify the hidden assumption, name the invariant that matters, and defend the design with evidence.

Let’s start by organizing the space. The main lecture topic branches into several failure patterns: race conditions, deadlock, missed signals, and livelock. Each of those should lead us toward evidence, not just intuition. And then evidence feeds design response. That is the professional loop here: identify the failure mode, capture the proof, and choose a correction that protects the right property without pretending the trade-off disappears.

A race condition begins with multiple writers and no protection. That can produce a lost update, stale state, or other results that look random but are actually explainable once timing is involved. A common mistake is to assume the method is correct because it worked once. The key idea here is to force the design to prove itself under repeated execution, because only then do we learn whether the state transition is actually safe.

This pattern is about reading state, deciding based on that read, and then acting after the state may already have changed. That gap is where the bug lives. The operation is built on a stale view, so the invariant can break even though every individual step seems reasonable. In practice, this is why we want the design to expose the transition explicitly and why we test with a repeatable scenario rather than a single clean run.

Deadlock is a circular resource dependency. One thread holds one resource and waits for another, while a second thread does the reverse, and now nothing moves. What makes this especially dangerous is that the system may appear active right up until it stops making progress. The engineering question is not just how to prevent the cycle, but how to recognize it in logs, traces, or blocked-worker evidence when it happens.

A missed signal happens when something is signaled before the receiver is actually waiting. The notification is effectively lost, and the waiting side can sit forever. This is a classic timing failure, and it is easy to miss in a baseline test because the timing has to line up just wrong. The fix is usually not magical; it is a guarded wait, a stronger state protocol, and evidence that shows the wakeup condition is handled correctly.

Livelock is different from deadlock: the system is busy, but it is not getting anywhere. You may see retries, backoffs that are too weak, or actors constantly changing state without ever completing the work. That is uncomfortable because activity can fool people into thinking the system is healthy. The thing to measure here is progress, not motion, and that is why a progress metric matters.

When we say evidence, we are being very specific. We want correlation IDs so we can trace one workflow, entity IDs so we know which object changed, state transitions so the narrative is reconstructable, and latency plus retry data so pressure is visible. Then we need a repeatable workload, because without repeatability we cannot compare the baseline to the fix. This is the kind of material that makes a failure defensible in review.

The design response starts with the invariant, not the tool. Once you know what must remain true, you choose the mechanism that protects it, such as a guarded transition, explicit coordination, or a retry-safe path. Then you make the transition visible, validate with a test, and defend the trade-off. The important point is that protection is never free: you usually pay with complexity, waiting, or reduced throughput.

Here is the practical comparison. A simple baseline is easy to explain, but it often hides timing assumptions. A guarded transition protects the invariant directly, but it requires careful state modeling. Explicit coordination makes dependencies visible, though it can add waiting. And observability-first design gives you strong evidence, but it means more instrumentation work. The right choice depends on what failure you are trying to make impossible, or at least measurable.
